The simplified cylindrical cloak has the following material parameters: μr = (r-a)/(b-a), μθ = 1, and εz = b^2/(b-a).

The zeroth-order wave equation for the simplified cloak can be simplified to the standard Bessel differential equation, indicating that the zeroth-order wave sees the cloak as a homogeneous isotropic medium.
Analytical solutions were obtained for the zeroth-order scattering coefficient, which was found to converge to 0.867 as the outer radius b is increased.
Numerical simulations showed that the higher-order scattering coefficients exhibit an oscillatory behavior and do not converge to zero even for thick cloak walls.
The simplified cloak cannot completely shield objects from electromagnetic illumination, as the zeroth-order cylindrical wave can penetrate into the cloak interior.
Compared to a near-ideal cloak, the simplified cloak has overall higher scattering, especially in the monopole (zeroth-order) wave component.
As the outer radius b is increased, the zeroth-order transmission coefficient converges to 1, indicating better transparency for this wave component.
The authors used the finite element method to numerically compute the scattering and transmission coefficients for the simplified cloak.
The operating frequency used in the case study was 2 GHz, with the inner and outer radii of the cloak set to 0.1 m and variable b, respectively.

The authors conclude that the simplified cloak is inherently visible and cannot provide perfect cloaking due to the transmission of the zeroth-order cylindrical wave and finite scattering of higher-order waves.
